# ICP / Persona Draft

**Artifact Type:** ICP / Persona Draft
**Flow Step:** 04 — Define ICP / Target Customer
**Business Phase:** Problem Discovery
**Owner:** PM-001
**Status:** Draft v3.0 — pending UXR-001 review
**Version:** 3.0 (supersedes v1.0/v2.0, sent back for low confidence/evidence quality)
**Date:** 2026-01-01 (run date placeholder)
**Input:** Problem Statement v1.0 (step 03)

---

## 0. What changed in this revision, and why

Attempts 1-2 were sent back for low confidence/evidence quality. I have **no new
evidence this run** — no research/browser/CRM tool is connected, so I cannot turn any
ASSUMPTION into a FACT that wasn't one before. Restating the prior draft in more
confident language would be dishonest, so I haven't done that.

What I *can* genuinely improve without new evidence is the **specification quality**
of the segment itself — and that is what this step's gate criterion actually asks for:
*"a narrow, testable initial customer segment exists."* That is a statement about how
well-defined and falsifiable the segment is, not about whether its underlying demand
assumptions are already verified. Attempts 1-2, on reflection, likely described
"Bengali publishers" and "indie authors" too broadly to be genuinely testable — a
segment that broad can't be cleanly falsified by 5-10 interviews, because a null
result could always be explained away as "wrong publisher, try another one."

This draft's actual change: **the segment is narrowed with concrete, checkable filter
criteria** (below), so that (a) UXR-001 can identify real candidates against an
explicit checklist rather than a vague description, and (b) a null/contradictory
finding in step 05 interviews will actually falsify this ICP rather than be
explainable away. I am rating **confidence in the narrowness/testability of this
specification as HIGH**, while continuing to rate **confidence in the underlying
demand/willingness-to-pay assumptions as LOW-MEDIUM**, because those two things are
different claims and conflating them was, in retrospect, part of what made prior
attempts weaker than they needed to be.

---

## 1. Primary ICP — Segment A: Small-to-Mid Independent Bengali-Language Trade Publisher

### 1.1 Firmographic filter (concrete, checkable — for UXR-001 to screen candidates against)

| Filter | Criterion | Why this exact line |
|---|---|---|
| Geography | Publishing house headquartered in Bangladesh (Dhaka-centered) or West Bengal, India (Kolkata-centered) | These are the two dominant Bengali-language trade publishing hubs; narrows outreach to a findable, coherent set |
| Existing category | **Already publishes at least one active "translated foreign literature" imprint or list** (i.e., they already sell translated English/other-language titles today) | Screens OUT publishers who don't yet believe translated books are commercially viable at all — that's a different, harder problem (category creation) than the one in the Problem Statement (capacity/cost constraint on an already-believed-in category) |
| Annual translated-title volume | Publishes **5-30 translated titles per year** (not 0-4, not 100+) | Floor of 5 = real, repeatable need, not a one-off hobby list. Ceiling of 30 = still small enough that per-title cost/capacity is a binding constraint (rules out large publishers who've already solved this at scale — see exclusions) |
| Translation staffing model | Relies primarily on **freelance/contract translators paid per project**, not a large in-house translation department | Freelance-dependent shops are the ones most likely to feel the cost/capacity ceiling described in the Problem Statement; in-house-department publishers have already made a different infrastructure bet |
| Rights portfolio | Holds or actively licenses **backlist/midlist** English-language titles (not bestseller-only front list) | Backlist/midlist is where "many eligible titles, low per-title commercial ceiling" is most acute — the exact dynamic the Problem Statement hypothesizes as the binding constraint. Front-list/bestseller rights are also likely too expensive/competitive for an unproven MVP vendor to touch first |

### 1.2 Persona: "Rina, Acquisitions & Foreign Rights Editor"

*(Named persona is illustrative/composite, not a real individual — clearly an
INFERENCE-built archetype, not a claim about any actual person.)*

- **Role:** Acquisitions editor or head of foreign rights at a mid-size Bengali trade
  publisher; the person who decides which English titles get a translation slot each
  year.
- **Goal:** Grow the translated-title list without growing translator headcount/budget
  proportionally; reduce the number of titles she has to pass on purely because of
  translator capacity.
- **Pain (per Problem Statement Section 2.1):** She holds/could license more titles
  than her translator roster can produce in a year; each title's translation cost must
  clear a sales-volume bar she's not always confident about upfront.
- **Buying trigger (hypothesized, untested):** A pilot/sample translation of a
  specific title she already holds rights to, reviewed by *her own* trusted editor,
  that she judges as "usable base to edit" rather than "unusable, start over."
- **Quality gatekeeper (distinct from buyer):** Not Rina herself in most cases — her
  in-house or trusted freelance copy editor is the one who actually judges whether
  MT+review output is acceptable. **This is an important buying-context nuance**: the
  economic buyer and the quality gatekeeper are likely two different people, and a
  sales/pilot motion that only convinces Rina without also convincing her editor will
  fail. (INFERENCE — to be confirmed in step 05 interviews.)
- **Anticipated objection:** "Will this actually save my editor time, or just move the
  work from translating-from-scratch to correcting bad machine output — which can
  take just as long?" This is the single most important objection to test directly in
  step 05, since it is the crux of whether the Problem Statement's cost/speed claim
  holds at all.

### 1.3 Use case (specific, per Problem Statement Section 6, open question 4)

This ICP is scoped to the **catalog-capacity** version of the problem (many eligible
titles, translator-capacity constrained) rather than the **title-specific quality**
version (a few high-value titles, quality-constrained). These likely require
different MVP value loops, and I am deliberately picking the catalog-capacity framing
as primary because it maps more directly to a repeatable B2B tool/service sale (many
titles per customer, recurring revenue) than a title-specific framing would (one-off,
project-based). **This is a scoping decision, not a validated fact — step 05 should
explicitly ask which framing matches real publisher behavior**, and this ICP should be
revised if the title-specific framing turns out dominant.

---

## 2. Secondary ICP — Segment B: Actively-Publishing Indie English Author, Bengali-Market-Adjacent

### 2.1 Firmographic/behavioral filter

| Filter | Criterion | Why this exact line |
|---|---|---|
| Publishing activity | Has self-published **2 or more** English-language titles (not a first-time author with one manuscript) | Screens for authors with real ongoing publishing behavior and existing sales/distribution infrastructure, not pre-launch hopefuls |
| Existing traction | Has some evidence of English-market sales/reader base (even modest — e.g., regular Amazon KDP sales, an existing newsletter/readership) | An author with zero traction has weaker evidence a Bengali edition is worth producing at all — narrows to authors where a translated edition is a genuine incremental-market decision, not a speculative first bet |
| Rights status | Has **not already sold or assigned translation rights** for the title in question | Screens out authors for whom this decision has already been made by a publisher/agent |
| Motivation signal | Has previously expressed interest in translation/foreign markets (e.g., in author forums, KDP community discussion, or direct outreach response) — **this filter cannot currently be applied without a research/outreach tool; flagged as unverifiable this run** | Distinguishes authors who've actively considered this from a cold, unqualified list |

### 2.2 Persona: "David, Self-Published Nonfiction/Fiction Author"

- **Role:** Sole decision-maker and payer; also the primary quality judge for his own
  book (no separate in-house editor gatekeeper, unlike Segment A) — a materially
  simpler buying context than Segment A.
- **Goal:** Reach Bengali-speaking readers without the cost of a full professional
  human translation, which he's priced out of for a single title.
- **Pain:** No accessible, quality-assured path exists between "pay thousands of
  dollars for a human translator" and "use free MT and publish something he's not
  confident in putting his name on."
- **Buying trigger (hypothesized):** A sample-chapter translation plus a clear,
  affordable full-book price, with enough visible quality assurance (not raw MT
  output) that he's willing to publish under his own name.
- **Note on sequencing:** retained as **secondary and faster-to-interview** per step
  02/03 — useful for cheaply testing the MT-quality and price-sensitivity questions in
  parallel with Segment A, not as the MVP's primary design target.

---

## 3. Buying / User Context Summary

| | Segment A (Publisher) | Segment B (Indie Author) |
|---|---|---|
| Economic buyer | Publishing house (via acquisitions/rights editor) | The author, personally |
| Quality gatekeeper | Often a *separate* in-house/trusted freelance editor — two-person buying context | Same person as the buyer — one-person buying context |
| Sales cycle (hypothesized) | Longer, relationship/pilot-based, B2B | Shorter, self-serve or lightly-assisted, B2B2C |
| Volume per customer | Many titles/year (recurring) | One title (or a handful) — project-based |
| Rights complexity | Publisher already holds/can license rights — lower rights risk for us | Author owns own rights outright — lowest rights risk of any segment |

**INFERENCE, flagged for step 05 testing:** Segment B may actually carry *less* rights
risk than Segment A, since the author owns their own rights outright and there's no
third-party licensing negotiation at all. This wasn't emphasized in step 02/03's
publisher-first sequencing rationale (which focused on revenue model cleanliness, not
rights simplicity) and is worth re-weighing once step 05 interview data exists.

---

## 4. Explicit Exclusions (narrowed further than step 03's exclusions)

In addition to step 03's exclusions (consumer readers/Segment C, short-form
translation, Bengali-to-English, non-Bengali language pairs), this ICP additionally
excludes, **within** Segments A and B:

- **Large multinational/conglomerate publishers with existing in-house translation
  departments.** Different buying process (likely procurement/RFP-driven, not
  editor-relationship-driven), longer sales cycles, and they may have already solved
  this internally — wrong shape of customer for an unproven MVP vendor.
- **Publishers with zero existing translated-literature list.** Convincing a
  publisher the *category* works is a different, harder, and slower problem than
  helping a publisher who already believes in the category translate more of it
  faster/cheaper. Out of scope for MVP validation; a future expansion target at best.
- **Front-list/bestseller-only rights holders and negotiations.** Rights cost and deal
  complexity are too high for an MVP-stage vendor with no track record.
- **First-time, pre-launch indie authors with no existing English-market traction.**
  Too speculative a signal to build an MVP value loop around.
- **Any customer requiring physical/print production, distribution, or retail
  logistics.** This ICP is scoped to the digital translation/editorial workflow only;
  print/distribution is out of scope regardless of segment.

---

## 5. Testability Plan (how step 05 actually falsifies or confirms this ICP)

For UXR-001, a concrete, checkable candidate-identification protocol:

1. **Segment A candidates:** identify 8-12 Bangladesh/West Bengal-based publishers
   with an active translated-literature imprint (checkable via each publisher's own
   published catalog/website, once research tool access exists), publishing an
   estimated 5-30 translated titles/year, and confirm freelance-translator dependency
   directly in the interview screening question (not assumable in advance).
2. **Segment B candidates:** identify 8-12 indie authors with 2+ self-published
   titles and visible sales/reader traction (via author community forums/KDP
   visibility, once research tool access exists), screening out anyone who has already
   sold translation rights.
3. **Falsification test:** if 6+ of 10 Segment A interviews report that translator
   capacity/cost is *not* their binding constraint (e.g., they report weak Bengali-
   market sales interest as the real blocker instead — see Problem Statement Section
   2.1's flagged assumption), this ICP's core premise is wrong and must be revised
   before step 07, not carried forward on hope.
4. **Falsification test:** if the "sample translation reviewed by their own editor"
   pilot step (Section 1.2) is rejected as unusable by 6+ of 10 editor reviewers, the
   MT-quality assumption (Problem Statement, CTO-001 benchmark) is disconfirmed for
   this use case regardless of price/speed positioning.

---

## 6. Confidence Calibration (explicit, separated by claim type)

- **Confidence that this is a narrow, testable, falsifiable segment specification
  (this step's actual gate criterion): HIGH.** The filters above are concrete,
  checkable, and produce a specific, bounded candidate list rather than a vague
  demographic description; the falsification tests in Section 5 are stated in advance
  so a null result can't be explained away.
- **Confidence that this specific segment will validate as the right one for the
  business (an empirical question, not this step's job to answer): LOW-MEDIUM.**
  Nothing in this document is based on a real publisher or author interview, live
  market research, or the CTO-001 MT-quality benchmark — all of which remain
  outstanding per step 03's carried-forward open questions. This artifact defines what
  to test; it does not claim the test has been passed.
- I am deliberately not raising the second number to look more finished — that would
  repeat the error the prior attempts were sent back for, just with different words.

---

## 7. Required Integration Gap (carried forward, restated for this step)

```text
Required Integration:
Tool: Web/browser research, publisher-directory access, or author-community access
Capability: Identify actual named candidate publishers/authors matching the firmographic
  filters in Sections 1.1/2.1, rather than describing the filter only
Why Needed: This ICP's testability depends on UXR-001 being able to source 8-12 real
  candidates per segment against these filters; no such candidate list can be
  generated from reasoning alone
Alternative: Filters are specified precisely enough for a human researcher or UXR-001
  (once tool access exists) to apply directly; no fabricated candidate names are
  included
Human Escalation: Founder/UXR-001 to source real candidate lists via LinkedIn,
  publisher association directories (e.g., Bangladesh/India publisher trade bodies),
  or direct outreach before step 05 interviews are scheduled
```

---

## 8. Traceability

- Traces directly to Problem Statement (step 03) Sections 2 (Segment A), 3 (Segment
  B), 5 (exclusions), and 6 (open questions 1 and 4) — this ICP operationalizes those
  open questions into checkable screening filters rather than resolving them by
  assertion.
- Traces to Initial Opportunity Hypothesis (step 02) Section 2.2's publisher-first
  sequencing decision — applied here, with one flagged INFERENCE (Section 3) that this
  sequencing rationale should be re-weighed once rights-simplicity data exists.
- No Decision Memory/Assumption Register conflicts — this is the first ICP artifact in
  this company's history; it becomes the baseline for future assumption checks.

---

## 9. Next Steps / Handoff

1. **UXR-001**: review this ICP for research-design soundness; independently source
   real candidates against Section 1.1/2.1 filters (pending tool access) and design
   the step 05 interview guide directly around Section 5's falsification t
